n: A new collection (chapters 25–29): proverbs of Solomon copied by scholars in King Hezekiah’s court, about 250 years after Solomon. Hezekiah was a reforming king who valued Israel’s heritage.

f.g: Reigned about 715–686 BC; a righteous king of Judah.

n: God’s glory includes mysteries beyond us; a king’s glory is to investigate matters carefully. God reveals in his time, and leaders must search diligently.

f.w: It is the glory of God to conceal a thing

n: Like the height of heaven and the depth of the earth, a king’s mind can’t be fully understood.
Remove the impurities from silver, and a craftsman can make something beautiful.

f.g: dross = impurities skimmed off molten metal.

n: Likewise, remove wicked advisers from the king, and his throne will be established in righteousness.

f.w: his throne shall be established in righteousness

n: Don’t push yourself forward in the king’s presence or claim a place among the great.

f.g: Don’t exalt yourself; don’t show off.

n: Better to be invited up than to be sent down in front of others. Jesus taught a parable about taking the lowest seat at a feast that echoes this.
Don’t rush to take someone to court; what will you do if your neighbor proves you wrong?

f.w: Go not forth hastily to strive

n: Settle your dispute privately with your neighbor, and don’t betray someone else’s confidence to win.

f.w: Debate thy cause with thy neighbour himself

n: Otherwise people will shame you, and your bad reputation will never go away.
A word spoken at the right moment is like golden apples set in silver—beautiful and precious.
Wise correction given to a listening ear is as lovely as gold jewelry.

f.w: a wise reprover upon an obedient ear

n: A faithful messenger refreshes those who send him like cool snow-water at harvest time. (Snow from Mount Hermon may have been used to cool drinks.)

f.w: the cold of snow in the time of harvest
f.g: A cooling drink during the heat of harvest—refreshing, not snowfall itself.

n: Someone who boasts of gifts he never gives is like clouds and wind that bring no rain—full of promise, empty of help.
Patience can persuade a ruler, and a gentle tongue can break bone—softness can overcome the hardest resistance.

f.w: a soft tongue breaketh the bone

n: Found honey? Eat just enough, or you’ll get sick. Good things are best in moderation.

f.w: eat so much as is sufficient for thee

n: Don’t visit your neighbor too often, or he’ll grow tired of you. Even friendship needs balance.

f.g: Don’t set foot there too often.

n: A false witness is as deadly as a war club, a sword, or a sharp arrow.

f.g: maul = a heavy club or hammer used as a weapon.

n: Relying on an unreliable person in a crisis is like chewing with a broken tooth or walking on a sprained foot—painful and useless.
Singing cheerful songs to a grieving person is like taking away their coat on a cold day or pouring vinegar on soda—it only stirs things up. Sensitivity matters more than cheerfulness.

f.g: nitre = soda (natron); vinegar on it fizzes violently.

n: If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if thirsty, give him water. Paul quotes this, and Jesus taught to love our enemies.
Kindness may burn with shame in his conscience and lead him to change, and the Lord will reward you. The “coals of fire” likely refer to remorse, not harm.

f.w: heap coals of fire upon his head
f.g: Likely a figure of burning shame or repentance stirred by unexpected kindness.

n: As the north wind brings rain, a sly tongue brings angry looks. (Some read: an angry look stops gossip.)

f.g: backbiting = speaking evil of someone behind their back.

n: Repeats 21:9: better a corner of the roof than a big house shared with a quarrelsome spouse.
Good news from far away is as refreshing as cold water to someone parched—precious in a world of slow travel.

f.w: good news from a far country

n: A righteous person who caves in to the wicked is like a muddied spring or polluted well—something that should give life is spoiled.

f.g: A spring muddied by trampling feet.

n: Too much honey is bad, and seeking your own glory isn’t glorious.

f.w: for men to search their own glory is not glory

n: A person without self-control is like a city with broken-down walls—defenseless against every attack.

f.w: He that hath no rule over his own spirit
